content: 1. Active Tuberculosis (TB) Disease Case: This refers to an individual who exhibits clinical signs or symptoms of active TB and has a positive test result for Mycobacterium tuberculosis through smear examination, culture, or a molecular diagnostic test recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), such as Xpert MTB/RIF. Alternatively, it includes cases where a clinician or medical practitioner has made a clinical diagnosis of TB and decided to initiate a full course of TB treatment. This term is synonymous with a confirmed TB case. 2. Advanced HIV Disease: For adults, adolescents, and children aged five years or older, advanced HIV disease is defined by a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of a WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 event at the time of care presentation. All children living with HIV who are younger than five years are considered to have advanced disease at presentation. 3. Aggregate Data: This type of data includes elements entered into a data system that represent a combination of individuals or services with shared characteristics. For example, it may include the number of positive HIV test results or the number of people tested within a specific age group, such as 15–19 years. 4. Confidentiality: This is the right of individuals to have their personal data protected during storage, transfer, and use, ensuring that unauthorized disclosure to third parties is prevented. 5. Data Element: A logical unit of data that has a specific name, a precise definition, and a set of permissible values (if applicable). Indicators are constructed using formulas that combine data elements and other components. 6. Differentiated Service Delivery (DSD): This is a person-centered approach that simplifies and adapts HIV services across the care continuum to meet the needs and preferences of people living with HIV or those vulnerable to infection. It also optimizes the use of available resources within health systems. 7. Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK): This is a standardized distillation of WHO guidelines and operational resources into formats that can be easily integrated into digital patient tracking and decision-support systems. It includes essential components such as workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, metrics, reporting indicators, and functional requirements for defined health program areas. 8. Electronic Health Information System: A computerized system used to store, manage, and analyze routine service data, including both aggregate and individual-level data. In these guidelines, the terms electronic and digital are used interchangeably. 9. Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) RNA: This refers to the viral genomes of HCV that can be detected and quantified in serum using nucleic acid testing. 10. HCV Core Antigen: This is the nucleocapsid peptide 22 (p22) of the hepatitis C virus, which is released into plasma during viral assembly. It can be detected early in the infection and throughout its course. 11. HCV Sustained Virological Response (SVR): This is defined as an undetectable level of HCV RNA in the blood at a specific time point after the completion of treatment, typically at 12 or 24 weeks (SVR12 or SVR24). 12. Health Information System (HIS): This system is used to manage data for decision-making related to the design or management of health services. It encompasses data collection, compilation, analysis, synthesis, and use. 13. HIV Care: This involves routine clinical assessment, monitoring, and management of HIV, including antiretroviral treatment (ART), tailored to the specific needs of the patient. 14. HIV Case Surveillance: This refers to the reporting of an initial diagnosis of HIV infection and defined sentinel events related to public health actions. It involves collecting critical data elements for program management and monitoring. 15. HIV Self-Testing (HIVST): This is a process where an individual collects their own specimen (oral fluid or blood) using a simple rapid HIV test kit, performs the test, and interprets the result at a time and place of their choosing. 16. Indicator: A quantitative or qualitative measure that provides a valid and reliable way to assess performance or reflect changes associated with an activity, project, or program. 17. Individual-Level Data: This refers to information related to a single person, potentially collected over time and across different points of care. It may include clinical or research data, such as information on an individual receiving HIV care at multiple service points, along with their sociodemographic characteristics. This type of data allows for longitudinal and multivariate analysis of indicators. 18. Infant Diagnosis: This involves testing infants and children to determine their HIV status following potential exposure during gestation, delivery, or breastfeeding. Early infant diagnosis refers to testing HIV-exposed infants before two months of age. For infants under 18 months, molecular (nucleic acid) technologies should be used, while serological assays are appropriate for children aged 18 months and older. 19. Integrated Care: This refers to the delivery of multiple health services or interventions to a patient during the same visit by a single health worker or clinical team. Integration within a patient monitoring system involves using a single folder, patient card, or electronic medical record to manage or monitor a patient’s care over time for multiple conditions (e.g., HIV, TB, pregnancy, diabetes). 20. Key Populations: These are defined groups at increased risk of HIV, viral hepatitis, or sexually transmitted infections (STIs) due to specific high-risk behaviors, regardless of the epidemic type or local context. They often face legal and social challenges that heighten their vulnerability. Key populations include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, people in prisons or closed settings, sex workers, and transgender or gender-diverse individuals. 21. Latent TB Infection (LTBI): This is a state of persistent immune response to stimulation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of clinically manifest active TB. Individuals with LTBI do not have active TB disease but may develop it in the future, a process known as TB reactivation. LTBI therapy is now referred to as TB preventive therapy. 22. Lay Provider: This is any individual who performs functions related to health care delivery and has been trained to provide specific services but has not received formal professional or paraprofessional certification or a tertiary degree. 23. Minimum Dataset: This is a standardized set of essential data elements relevant for patient or client management and program monitoring. It defines the key data to be collected by a health information system through paper, electronic, or mobile devices. The minimum dataset captures key events in an individual’s interaction with the health system along the HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and related health services cascade. It is used to calculate priority indicators for program management and monitoring. 24. New TB Case: This refers to an individual who has never received treatment for TB or has taken anti-TB drugs for less than one month. 25. Partner Services: Also known as disclosure, contact tracing, index testing, or partner notification, this is a voluntary process where a trained provider asks individuals diagnosed with HIV about their sexual or drug-injecting partners. With the client’s consent, the provider offers these partners voluntary HIV testing services (HTS). Partner services can be delivered through provider-assisted referral or patient referral approaches. 26. Patient Management: This involves the provision of care and treatment in consultation with a patient over time. It may also be referred to as patient care, clinical management, or clinical monitoring. 27. Person-Centered Health Services: This approach consciously adopts the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities who are the intended beneficiaries of health services. It views them as participants and beneficiaries of trusted health systems that respond to their needs and preferences in humane and holistic ways. 28. Person-Centered Monitoring: This involves the routine collection, compilation, and analysis of data on health service clients over time and across service delivery points. Its primary purpose is to guide the continuity of clinical management for a person over time and across locations. In the context of HIV, this approach shifts from measuring services (e.g., the number of HIV tests administered) to measuring support for individuals receiving HIV services (e.g., the number of people tested or who know their HIV status). 29. Point-of-Care Testing (POC): This refers to testing conducted at the site where clinical care is provided, with results returned to the individual or their caregiver on the same day as sample collection and testing. This enables timely clinical decision-making. 30. Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP): HIV PrEP involves the use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs by individuals who are not infected with HIV to prevent acquiring the virus. 31. Privacy: In this context, privacy refers to the legal protection granted to individuals to control access to and use of their personal information. It provides the overall framework within which confidentiality and security are implemented. 32. Programme Management: This includes real-time direction and decision-making for multifaceted health program services and resources, based on health information about program inputs, outputs, outcomes, and impact. 33. Programme Monitoring: This involves the routine tracking and reporting of priority information about a program, including its outputs, quality, gaps, and outcomes, typically in relation to a national plan, goals, and targets. 34. Rapid ART Initiation: This refers to the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) within seven days of an HIV diagnosis. 35. Relapse TB Case: This refers to an individual who has previously been treated for TB, was declared cured or had completed treatment, and is now diagnosed with a recurrent episode of TB. This may be due to reactivation of the original infection or reinfection. It does not include individuals who failed previous treatment or returned to treatment after a prolonged interruption. 36. Repeat Testing: This occurs when additional testing is performed immediately following an initial test during the same visit due to inconclusive or discrepant results. The same assay(s) and, where possible, the same specimen are used. 37. Retesting: This involves testing a second specimen from the same individual at a different time point, following the same testing algorithm. Retesting may also be conducted to verify an HIV-positive diagnosis before ART initiation as a quality assurance step. 38. Routine Surveillance: In public health, surveillance refers to the continuous, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health-related data needed for planning, implementing, and evaluating public health practices. Surveillance builds on routine data, including patient or client monitoring, and incorporates additional data to describe the overall health context for public health action.
